author: Clif Droke
title: Recession Is Not Imminent
text:
Economists are on high alert over the possibility of a recession in 2019. Strenuous relations between the U.S. and its chief trading partners, coupled with continued deterioration in the emerging markets, have led to increased concerns that the global slowdown could trip up the U.S. economy this year. In this report we’ll examine the leading indicators for clues as to whether or not the domestic economy will survive the global slowdown. We’ll see that while there are definitely some areas of concern, the bulk of the indicators point to the U.S. dodging the recession bullet in 2019.
As if the U.S.-China trade war wasn’t enough to induce jitters among investors, the 20% drop in the S&P 500 Index (SPX) into bear market territory did even more to stoke recession fears. Many investors believe the canard about the stock market being able to accurately predict recessions, but as we’ve experienced many times over the past few decades, this isn’t always true. The Wall Street bromide, “The stock market has predicted nine of the last five recessions,” comes to mind.
Nonetheless, it would be equally foolish to dismiss a 20% decline in the S&P 500 as having no economic validity at all. The SPX is, after all, a component of the Conference Board’s Leading Economic Index. The S&P 500 can be considered as forward-looking in that it reflects the market’s expectations for business conditions, interest rates, and the economy.
With that in mind, let’s not be so quick to dismiss the recent underperformance of the equity market and its relationship to the economy. In my experience, there are specific stocks and industry groups which are extremely sensitive to changes in consumer expectations and therefore provide valuable insights into the near-term future of the U.S. economy. Let’s take a look at some of them.
One of the main drivers behind the strong consumer spending levels up until recently has been the upper-middle class income stratum. This socioeconomic group is comprised of individuals earning in excess of $100,000 per year, or couples earning roughly $250,000 or more annually. Upper middle class consumers tend to be freer with their spending than the middle class and are an important component of U.S. economic growth.
One valuable reflection of the spending patterns of this economic class is a stock price composite which I call the Upper Middle Class Index. The Upper Middle Class Index averages several stocks of companies that cater primarily to an upper-middle class customer base. Components of this index include Target ( TGT ), Starbucks ( SBUX ), Bavarian Motor Works ( OTCPK:BMWYY ), Ruth’s Hospitality Group ( RUTH ), and Apple Inc. ( AAPL ).
The thinking behind this index is that it serves as a reflection of the spending patterns of upper-middle class Americans; therefore as goes the collective trend of these stocks, so goes the consumer sentiment of the upper-middle class. When the Upper Middle Class Index is in decline, it implies that upper middle Americans are reigning in their spending and therefore concerned about the future of the economy. Shown below is the Upper Middle Class Index updated as of Jan. 4.
Source: WSJ
As you can see here, the Upper Middle Class Index has decisively broken under a multi-year uptrend in recent weeks and, for the first time since late 2015, is showing signs of major weakness. This is by no means a guarantee that recession will arrive in the U.S. in coming months, but it's nonetheless a "heads up" that an important group of consumers are retrenching.
Even more important than the upper middle, however, is America's middle class. Collectively, this group of consumers constitute the bulk of spending in the economy and are therefore the group to which economists should devote most of their attention to. With all the talk about a possible recession, one would logically expect the average working class American to be hit the hardest by such a development. Yet there are signs that while the middle class has curtailed their spending to some extent in recent months, they don’t seem overly concerned by all the negatives swirling around the financial market.
For proof of this, consider the Middle Class Index shown below. This indicator is my favorite measure of the strength of the middle class retail economy. This indicator is a stock price composite of several leading companies which cater to a predominantly middle income clientele, including such companies as Walmart ( WMT ), Dollar General ( DG ) and Ford ( F ). Normally this indicator shows weakness when intermediate-term U.S. economic growth prospects are sluggish, but the Middle Class Index is still in a rising trend and not far from a 4-year high.
Source: WSJ
What this suggests is that middle income Americans aren't retrenching to the degree that the upper middle class are. From this observation we can deduce that the U.S. economy isn't in any imminent danger of entering recession. Recessions are generally the result of the middle class significantly cutting back on spending. That's evidently not the case right now.
Now let's examine the New Economy Index (NASDAQ: NEI ). This is my indicator for measuring the strength of the U.S. retail sector in real time. This index is comprised of some of the biggest stocks reflective of the U.S. retail, employment and transportation segments of the economy. Among the components are Amazon ( AMZN ), eBay ( EBAY ) and FedEx ( FDX ). Here's what the New Economy Index looks like as of Jan. 4.
Source: WSJ
I've long considered the NEI to be an accurate leading indicator of a slowdown in the consumer retail sector. The rule for interpreting this index is that when the NEI price line falls below its nearest pivotal low, followed by a downward trend in the 12-week (red line) and 20-week (black line) moving averages for at least 2-3 weeks, a reversal of trend has been confirmed for the U.S. retail economy. This index proved invaluable in 2007 by predicting the slowdown ahead of the 27 by predicting the slowdown ahead of the 2008 recession and with the brief exception of the 2010 "flash crash", it hasn't given a confirmed breakdown signal until now. As with the Upper Middle Class Index, I wouldn't put too much weight on this indicator in isolation when it comes to predicting a recession. However, the recent breakdown in NEI does at least tell us that conditions in the U.S. retail sector are slowing and could potentially worsen in the coming months.
Now that we've reviewed the leading signals in the equity market, let's turn our attention to the more classical measures of economic strength and weakness. Shown below is the Conference Board Employment Trends Index. Although the index declined in November, the rate of change in this index has been amazingly positive. As you can see here, the growth trend and momentum behind this index has been powerful to the upside and shows no signs of slowing down. This is one of the most important indications of whether or not a recession is likely in the coming 6-9 months.
Source: Econintersect
Another important indication of present economic strength, and therefore a recession indicator, is business lending. Shown here is a graph courtesy of the St. Louis Fed showing commercial and industrial lending activity in the last few years. The rising trend shows no signs of slowing, even when viewed on a year-over-year basis. Historically, recessions are signaled when the 12-month rate of change in this indicator turns south. As of early January, the rate of change is still rising.
Source: St. Louis Fed
Of the five leading indicators reviewed here, only two are showing major signs of weakness - namely the Upper Middle Class Index and the New Economy Index. The other three - the Middle Class Index, the Employment Trends Index and the Commercial and Industrial Loans trend, which arguably are of greater importance than the former two, are still strong. With three of five leading indicators in a position of strength, I can only conclude that an economic recession is not likely to occur in the coming 6-9 months.
With this in mind, investors should avoid falling victim to recession fears and instead concentrate on taking advantage of what should be a profitable next few months. The stock market is dramatically "oversold" and valuations are still attractive, thus there are opportunities for deploying capital in stocks the intermediate term which should benefit from the residual economic strength reflected in the above mentioned indicators. In short, now is the time for optimism, not pessimism.
